column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
Compare the flow of water in a river with what happens in a wire carrying a current. What is flowing, and how do we say how much of it passes?
A torch does not light until you press its button. What is that button doing to the path of the current?
Which way do the charge carriers in a metal wire actually move compared with the direction we draw for the current, and why do we have this convention?
A wire carries 3 coulombs past a point every second. How many amperes is that, and what does the unit mean?
Where in a circuit do you put the meter that reads the current, and why does that place make sense?
A pipe lying perfectly level with water in it does not flow. What is the equivalent of a raised tank for electricity in a wire?
Where does the push that keeps a current flowing in a torch come from, and what gets used up over time?
What is happening to the charge, in terms of energy, when it passes through a 6 volt battery, and what does 'volt' measure?
How do you connect a meter to read the potential difference across a bulb, compared with how you connect the one for current?
If you doubled the number of cells across a nichrome wire and plotted the readings, what shape of graph would you get?
What condition must hold for the potential difference across a wire to be exactly proportional to the current in it?
Why does a metal wire not let electrons rush through with no hindrance, and what do we call the hindrance and its unit?
How can you dim a bulb without changing the battery, and what happens to the current when you do?
You have two pieces of the same metal: one long and thin, one short and thick. Which will let more current flow, and why?
If a wire is stretched to twice its length at the same cross-section, how does its resistance compare, and which constant of the material stays the same?
What is it about the material itself, and not the shape of the wire, that tells us whether it is a good conductor or an insulator?
Explain why a toaster's coil is made of a mixture of metals instead of pure copper, while the cable bringing power to the house is copper or aluminium.
If you move an ammeter between different resistors of a series circuit, what happens to its reading, and why?
Three resistors in series are connected across a battery. How are the voltage across the whole combination and the voltages across each resistor related?
A 20 ohm lamp and a 4 ohm conductor are placed in series. How would you find the single resistance that could replace them, and how does it compare with each?
A voltmeter across each branch of a parallel combination reads an identical value. Why is that?
A 12 V battery drives three resistors of 5, 10 and 30 ohm in parallel. How would you find the current from the battery?
Connecting more resistors in parallel across a source, does the total resistance rise or fall, and what rule gives the exact value?
Why do festival fairy lights wired one after another take so long to repair when one bulb goes, and what else is wrong with that arrangement for a bulb and a heater?
What lets a fan, a bulb and a heater share the same mains supply and each get the right current?
Why does a fan feel warm after long use and an electric heater get hot, and how do the two differ in where the energy goes?
If the current through a heating coil doubles with everything else fixed, by what factor does the heat in the same time change, and why?
Name some household appliances that make use of the heat a current produces, and one place where that heat is unwanted.
What properties must the wire inside a bulb have, which metal is chosen, and why is the bulb not simply filled with air?
A faulty appliance suddenly draws far more current than normal. How does a fuse in its circuit protect the house wiring?
A bulb is marked 60 W and a heater 1500 W. What does that tell you about how each uses electrical energy?
A 400 W refrigerator runs 8 hours a day. How would you work out the energy used in a month, in the unit the electricity board charges for?
